additions.title: Enforcement Notice: Serco Leisure Operating Limited
additions.locator: Paras 29 to 33 and 39 (lawful basis); background sub-paragraph (e) on the timing of the legitimate interests assessment
additions.quote: Serco cannot rely on Article 6(1)(f) as it has failed to demonstrate the necessity of the processing
additions.why: A UK enforcement decision that tests a claimed lawful basis and rejects it. The employer relied on contract and legitimate interests for facial recognition and fingerprint attendance checks; the regulator found neither applied because less intrusive means existed and the balancing test gave too little weight to staff. The legitimate interests assessment was done after roll-out and after the regulator made contact. Limits: an enforcement notice, filed under 'regulator guidance' because the type list has no value for one; about biometric recognition of employees, not model training; the notice orders the processing to stop and is not a fine.

additions.title: The Information Commissioner v Clearview AI Incorporated [2025] UKUT 319 (AAC)
additions.locator: Summary of decision; Decision; the description of the system ending at para 43
additions.quote: utilises 'crawlers' to 'scrape' the public-facing internet for images of human faces
additions.why: The tribunal ruling behind the brief's figure. It holds that the UK regulator had jurisdiction over a United States company that scraped faces from the internet to build a machine-learning recognition service, and sends the substantive appeal back to be heard. So the question of whether there was any lawful basis can now be decided. Limits: decides jurisdiction only, not lawful basis; the quoted words are from the summary, which is not part of the decision; a further appeal was reported in December 2025 and its outcome was not checked in this pass. Used by another brief for a different passage.

additions.title: Guidelines 1/2024 on processing of personal data based on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR (version 1.0, for public consultation)
additions.locator: Para 9; executive summary, p. 2 (three cumulative conditions)
additions.quote: Article 6(1)(f) GDPR cannot be considered as a legal basis "by default".
additions.why: The European regulators' method for the legitimate interests test, in terms that match the criterion's second level: the basis may not be chosen automatically or stretched because it looks less demanding, and the assessment comes before the processing. Limits: the version adopted for public consultation; whether a final version has replaced it was not confirmed. EU guidance, not binding in the UK, and it does not cover the UK's recognised legitimate interests basis.

additions.title: Relying on the legal basis of legitimate interests to develop an AI system
additions.publisher: Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL)
additions.locator: Opening summary; section on the three conditions (legitimate interest, necessity, balance)
additions.quote: Controllers will most commonly rely on their legitimate interests for the development of AI systems.
additions.why: The most developed regulator guidance found on lawful basis for building AI. The French regulator accepts legitimate interests as the usual basis for development, subject to three conditions and safeguards, and recommends documenting the analysis; it lists interests that will not qualify. A more permissive tone than the UK regulator's 2024 position on web scraping. Limits: French regulator, EU GDPR; the page is a courtesy translation and says the French text prevails. Not binding in the UK.

additions.title: Guidance on privacy and developing and training generative AI models
additions.publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
additions.locator: 'Top five takeaways', second and third points
additions.quote: Just because data is publicly available or otherwise accessible does not mean it can legally be used to train or fine-tune generative AI models
additions.why: International comparator. Australian law has no list of lawful bases, yet the regulator reaches the same practical point: public availability is not permission, sensitive information generally needs consent, and reuse of data already held for training must be within what people would reasonably expect. Limits: Australian Privacy Act, not UK law; regulator guidance, not a decision.

additions.title: Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in AI Recommendation and Decision Systems
additions.locator: Part I, executive summary (p. 3); Part III, sections 4 to 6 (pp. 5-9)
additions.quote: organisations can rely on exceptions to consent under the PDPA, e.g., for business improvement or research purposes
additions.why: Second comparator, chosen because it takes a different legal route to the same question. Singapore starts from consent and then allows named exceptions for developing and testing AI, with criteria for each. Useful contrast with the UK approach of choosing among bases. Limits: advisory, expressly not legally binding; Singapore law; covers recommendation and decision systems, not generative models.

additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 13: Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
additions.quote: the purposes of the processing for which the personal data are intended as well as the legal basis for the processing
additions.why: The binding rule that makes lawful basis a matter of record, not afterthought: at the point of collection the controller must tell the person the legal basis and, where it is legitimate interests, what those interests are. A basis chosen after launch cannot have been disclosed on time. Limits: applies to data collected from the person; data obtained elsewhere, such as scraped data, falls under Article 14, which was not read in this pass.

additions.title: A Common Pool of Privacy Problems: Legal and Technical Lessons from a Large-Scale Web-Scraped Machine Learning Dataset
additions.publisher: Rachel Hong and five co-authors (University of Washington and others), arXiv
additions.locator: Section 7.3.1 'Lawful basis / consent'; contributions list in section 1
additions.quote: this basis requires a balancing test weighing the impact on individuals' rights
additions.why: Empirical audit of a 12.8 billion sample web-scraped training set, followed by legal analysis. The authors found personal information that filtering had not removed, including an estimated 136,000 or more images of CVs, and conclude that under the GDPR only legitimate interests or consent could support such a dataset, with the balance likely to go against the developer. Evidence for the 'training' limb of the criterion. Limits: read as an arXiv preprint (the page links a later conference version, not read); authors are US-based and the GDPR analysis is brief.

additions.title: Generative AI in EU Law: Liability, Privacy, Intellectual Property, and Cybersecurity
additions.publisher: Claudio Novelli, Federico Casolari, Philipp Hacker, Giorgio Spedicato and Luciano Floridi, arXiv
additions.locator: Privacy and data protection section, list of seven problems and sub-section 1 'Legal basis for AI training on personal data'
additions.quote: the appropriate legal basis for AI training; the appropriate legal basis for processing prompts
additions.why: Working paper that treats the legal basis for training and the legal basis for the data people type in as two separate questions, which is the structure the criterion uses. Also notes that the transparency duty requires the basis to be stated. Limits: preprint (version 4, March 2024); journal publication not confirmed in this pass; EU law, written before the EDPB's December 2024 opinion and before the UK's 2025 Act.

rejected.title: CJEU, Case C-621/22 Koninklijke Nederlandse Lawn Tennisbond (commercial interest as a legitimate interest) and Case C-252/21 Meta Platforms v Bundeskartellamt
rejected.reason: Not attempted separately: Curia returns a script shell and EUR-Lex HTTP 202 with an empty body (tested today on another case). Not read, not cited.

rejected.title: King and others, User Privacy and Large Language Models: An Analysis of Frontier Developers' Privacy Policies (2025)
rejected.reason: Read (abstract). Finds six US developers train on user chats by default, but the analysis is under Californian law and does not address lawful basis. Not kept; relevant to transparency.

rejected.title: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, Principles for responsible, trustworthy and privacy-protective generative AI technologies
rejected.reason: Reachable; not read in full. Two comparators already kept; not added to avoid padding.

rejected.title: UK GDPR, Article 21: Right to object
rejected.reason: Reachable; relevant to legitimate interests but one step removed from choosing a basis. Article 13 kept instead.

rejected.title: A standard or reporting framework on lawful basis
rejected.reason: None found that is free to read and speaks to lawful basis. ISO/IEC 27701 is a paid standard and was not opened. No reporting framework is relevant.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. Two points of drift to watch: (1) the French regulator's January 2026 guidance treats legitimate interests as the usual basis for AI development, a more permissive tone than the UK regulator's 2024 statement that developers will struggle with the balancing test; the UK position itself was not seen to have changed. (2) The brief's Clearview figure rests on a penalty still in litigation; the status after December 2025 was not rechecked in this pass.
